title: Choice, memory, and progressive disclosure
outcome: Reduce decision effort while keeping useful options discoverable.
useCase: Export dialogs, status menus, and complex settings.
benefits: Makes choices easier without arbitrarily deleting capability.
drawbacks: Disclosure and defaults can hide important options if poorly chosen.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Less uncertainty, not merely fewer buttons.

trace.title: User decision
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

A menu is a decision problem. Hick–Hyman-style findings relate choice time to uncertainty in controlled tasks.

They do not prove that every product should hide options or use exactly a certain number of buttons. Familiarity, grouping, labels, and task frequency matter.

Support recognition instead of forcing recall: show the available statuses, recent queues, or selected filters. Working memory is limited, but “seven items” is not a universal navigation rule.

Reduce the information a person must carry across steps.

Progressive disclosure puts common decisions first and exposes less common detail when needed. It works only if people can find the extra options and understand what is hidden.

An “Advanced” drawer should not conceal a setting most users need to finish the basic task.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Observe where hesitation comes from: too many choices, unfamiliar labels, fear of consequences, or missing information. These need different repairs.

Compare a grouped menu with a flat one using realistic tasks. Measure completion and wrong selections, not only how quickly someone clicks any option.

Faster mistakes are not an improvement.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
Hiding every option can increase search and memory burden. A default can help but can also cause a silent wrong choice.

Do not use a cognitive “law” as a substitute for context.
